summary: A note from SRI-ARC on how the NIC Journal would use FTP for mail delivery and submission. SRI first planned to hide parameters in the username field of MLFL, but the Network Mail Meeting preferred changing FTP so that parameters are stated explicitly. It describes what the NIC wanted.

plainLanguage.summary: The NIC wanted FTP to carry Journal articles and mail. This note describes explicit commands for message details instead of encoding them inside a user name.

questions: how to use ftp for journal
subtitle: SRI-ARC's proposed FTP commands for submitting and delivering NIC Journal mail.

tldr.problem: The NIC needed FTP support for Journal submissions and delivery, including message details that should not be hidden inside a user name.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes explicit mail subcommands for titles, authors, acknowledgments, recipients, mail class, recording, preservation, and sending text or a file citation.
tldr.outcome: The note describes desired FTP features conceptually and leaves exact syntax and dialogue order for later discussion.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 479 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. It describes conceptual requirements for the NIC Journal's use of FTP.

sections.title: Journal Use of FTP
sections.content:
James E. White explains how SRI-ARC hoped to use FTP's MLFL command for NIC Journal submission and delivery. Before a Network Mail meeting, the NIC had considered placing required parameters inside the FTP user-name field.

Participants at the meeting favored modifying FTP so each parameter could be declared explicitly. This RFC describes the commands the NIC would like to see, without fixing their exact syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC first considered hiding Journal instructions in a user name. The meeting favored separate commands that state those instructions clearly.

sections.title: Message Details and Recipients
sections.content:
The proposed subcommands include TITLE, human-readable and process-readable author information, acknowledgment details, and ADDRESSEES-ARE for recipients. Recipients could be identified by NIC Ident, a user name and host, or a name the NIC could look up.

MAIL-CLASS describes size and importance, while RECORD asks a server to record the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands could identify the writer and recipients, describe the message, and request an acknowledgment or a Journal record. Recipients could be named in several ways.

sections.title: Sending Text or a Citation
sections.content:
The proposal distinguishes a message's text from a file that can be retrieved elsewhere. TEXT sends the message text, while FILE identifies a file and host from which the content can be retrieved.

The RFC also describes a PRESERVED-AT statement for identifying a stored copy, and notes that some commands were then specific to the NIC's planned forwarding and recording service.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender could transmit the message itself or point to a file containing it. The RFC also describes how to identify where a preserved copy can be found.
